new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both quoted passages are present verbatim in the copies we hold; the only differences are locator conventions. (1) PDF page 5 (printed folio 4), footnote 3 reads exactly "Zaar and Gùùs (Sigidi) have 3 tone levels; the other languages have 2. Hi is marked with an acute accent; Lo with a grave; Mid is left unmarked." (verified on a rendered PNG of the page and in the extracted text, line 215 of the). The same claim appears in the body on p.3 (folio 2): "Zaar and Gùùs have three tone levels, the others only two." (2) : PDF page 14 (printed folio 13), point 3 reads exactly "Other languages have used tone to oppose the singular and the plural: Zakshi opposes High tones for singular to Low tones…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source says anything about word stress. Caron's first-hand South-Bauchi-West data establish only that Zakshi (and, by the group statement, the other non-Zaar/Guus lects including Boto and Zari) is a two-level tone language (High vs Low), with lexical and grammatical tone (e.g. High-toned singular vs Low-toned plural subject pronouns in Zakshi).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the two-tone statement is made at the group level ('the other languages have 2'), the Zakshi-specific evidence is the pronoun-tone paradigm.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level footnote about tone levels in a paper on pronominal/TAM systems; no phonology section, no word-prosody description of Zari, Zakshi or Boto exists in any opened source.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data come from Zakshi (Glottolog dialect zaks1239, spoken around Kundum), which Caron classifies in the Saya cluster alongside Boto (boto1248, Gindiri area) and Zari proper (Kopti/Kwapm, Padan Zari/Bangwon Zari) - the three varieties Ethnologue/Glottolog lump as Zari [zaz] zari1242. The two-tone statement is group-level ('the other [SBW] languages have 2'), Zakshi-specific evidence is the H(sg)/L(pl) pronoun paradigm. Note the vitality conflict: Ethnologue/Wikipedia call zaz extinct (last speaker before 2000) while Caron 2005/2009 report Zakshi as 'sound' with about 500 speakers (Boto likewise); the 'extinct' label can apply at most to Zari proper. Glottolog's single 'grammar sketch' for zari1242 (Caron 2003 'A linguist's field notes') is a mis-typed travel narrative about the Zaar field trip, and Glottolog itself flags it 'Not sure what this is.'
